failure_mode: LLM writes `try do … after <pattern> -> body end` — clause syntax (borrowed from `receive`'s `after N ->` / `rescue e ->`) inside `try`'s `after`, which is a plain expression block, not a clause-based construct. The file PARSES (Elixir accepts do/else/catch/rescue/after as generic keyword-block options on any call) and fails only during expansion with `error: misplaced operator ->` at the arrow's exact {line, column}. Real and observable. Note the repair is intent-ambiguous, not merely unimplemented: the "obvious" repair (drop the pattern head, keep the body) leaves the pattern-bound variables undefined, and the alternative repair (`after` -> `else`, which compiles and preserves the bindings) silently changes runtime semantics from run-always to run-on-success-only.
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/syntax/fix_after_clause_pattern_arrow.ex and its two tests; no rebuild ticket needed — the failure mode is already recorded verbatim in FAILURE_MODE_CATALOGUE.md cluster 13 (line 226, `try do … after {result, new_state} -> body end` → `misplaced operator ->`, plus the undefined-variable trap), and that cluster's highest-value catch was already assigned elsewhere (`no_if_else_in_receive_after`).

caught_by: elixir-compiler (partially — emits `incompatible types given to Kernel.apply/3` only when the receiver's type is inferrable; nothing for the untyped-field case this rule targets). No live credence rule matches it.
failure_mode: Calling a stored zero-arity function reference via `Kernel.apply/3` with a hallucinated function name — `apply(state.clock, :call, [])` — instead of the dot-call `state.clock.()`. `Kernel.apply/3` requires a module atom as its first argument, so passing a function value raises `ArgumentError` ("you attempted to apply a function named :call on #Function<...>") at runtime. Real and verified by execution. Its catchability splits in two: when the receiver's type is locally inferrable (literal `fn`, a local variable bound to a fn, a capture) Elixir 1.20 already emits `incompatible types given to Kernel.apply/3`; when the receiver is an untyped map/struct field — the exact shape this rule targets — the compiler emits nothing AND the construct is statically undecidable, because `apply(cfg.mod, :call, [])` is *correct* code when the field holds a module atom (verified: returns :from_module).
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/semantic/fix_apply_on_function_reference.ex and both test files; do not rebuild — record the failure mode as compiler-covered where decidable (`incompatible types given to Kernel.apply/3`) and statically undecidable where not, since `apply(cfg.mod, :call, [])` on a module-valued field is valid code the rule would corrupt.

failure_mode: LLM-generated Elixir uses the Bitwise infix operator spellings (`|||`, `&&&`, `<<<`, `>>>`, `~~~`, `^^^`) without `import Bitwise`. The code PARSES fine (verified `Code.string_to_quoted` = `:ok` for all six), but the compiler rejects it at expansion with `undefined function |||/2 (expected T1 to define such a function or for it to be imported, but none are available)` → `CompileError`, so the module never builds. The moduledoc's mechanism ("not recognised by the parser, which emits a syntax-error diagnostic") is false; the real construct is an unresolved-import error, and the same-answer repair is rewriting to the `Bitwise.bor/band/bsl/bsr/bnot/bxor` module calls, which need no import and stay guard-safe.

failure_mode: LLM treats `&1` as a magrittr-`.`/Clojure-`%` positional placeholder and pipes a block expression into a non-callable term: `if c do ... end |> {state, &1}`. The file PARSES; `Kernel.|>/2` raises at macro-expansion time with `ArgumentError: cannot pipe <lhs> into {state, &1}, can only pipe into local calls foo(), remote calls Foo.bar() or anonymous function calls foo.()`. Observable consequence: total compile failure of the module — loud, immediate, and the message names the offending operand verbatim. Correct repair is to bind the block to a variable and substitute it for `&1`.

failure_mode: Scope-model error in `cond`: an LLM assigns a variable in one `cond` branch body and references it in a LATER branch's guard, expecting sequential/nested scoping (the stab parser is indentation-insensitive, so visually-nested `->` clauses are flattened into siblings). Each `cond` clause is its own scope, so the compiler emits `error: undefined variable "user_key"` at the guard's position plus `warning: variable "user_key" is unused` at the assignment. Observable consequence: the module does not compile.

failure_mode: What this rule ENCODES is not an error. Its match?/1 source-gate accepts exactly `var = cond/case/if do ... end` followed by a statement using `var` — the already-correct hoisted idiom. In Elixir the block's value binds `var` in the enclosing scope; nothing is undefined. The moduledoc inverts real Elixir scoping. The adjacent REAL mode — assignment INSIDE each branch (`cond do a -> total = 0; true -> total = Enum.sum(v) end` then `total * 2`) → `error: undefined variable "total"` — is real but is precisely the shape this rule's gate REJECTS (probe: match? = false on it, fix/2 = no-op). That real mode is already caught+fixed for `case` by the live Credence.Semantic.FixCaseBranchAssignmentScope; its `cond`/`if` variants are uncaught and already catalogued (FAILURE_MODE_CATALOGUE.md lines 178-188), so nothing new is lost by deleting this module.

caught_by: Credence.Semantic.UndefinedFunction (detection only — it matches the diagnostic and reports rule: :undefined_function, but its fix/2 returns the source unchanged, so the deprecation is reported and never repaired)
failure_mode: LLM-generated code calls `Map.map(map, fn {k, v} -> new_value end)`, which has been soft-deprecated since Elixir 1.14. The compiler emits a real warning: "Map.map/2 is deprecated. Use Map.new/2 instead (invoke Map.from_struct/1 before if you have a struct)". The code still runs correctly; the defect is a deprecation warning that will become a hard removal. The trap the rule falls into is that the two functions are NOT interchangeable: Map.map/2's callback returns the new VALUE, Map.new/2's callback must return a {key, value} PAIR — so a bare Mod.fun rename silently changes the program's answer or crashes it at runtime, and Map.new/2 additionally cannot accept a struct receiver at all.
action: Delete lib/semantic/fix_deprecated_map_map.ex and its two tests from credence_evolution; do not port. If auto-repair of Map.map/2 is ever wanted, add a new wrap-callback replacement type (e.g. {:rename_wrap_pair, "Map", "new"}) to Credence.Semantic.UndefinedFunction's @qualified_replacements — gated to non-struct receivers and single-clause `fn {k, v} -> body end` callbacks — rather than introducing a competing rule that hijacks the dispatch slot.

caught_by: Credence.Syntax.FixDivRem — the LIVE rule of the identical name at /home/kamil/projects/credence/lib/syntax/fix_div_rem.ex (it fires, but its fix is itself incorrect; see evidence)
failure_mode: LLM-generated Elixir writes integer division/modulo as a Python-style infix word operator — `expected_sum = n * (n + 1) div 2`, `x = a rem 2 == 0`. `div`/`rem` are ordinary functions, not operators. Consequence is bimodal, and BOTH modes are real: (a) when the left operand ends in `)` or a literal, the file is a hard parse error — `Code.string_to_quoted("x = n * (n + 1) div 2")` => `{:error, {[line: 1, column: 17], "syntax error before: ", "'div'"}}`; (b) when the left operand is a bare identifier, it PARSES SILENTLY as a parenless call chain — `def half(n), do: n div 2` parses to `{:def, _, [{:half,...}, [do: {:n, _, [{:div, _, [2]}]}]]}`, i.e. `n(div(2))`, which then fails at compile/run time as an undefined function, not as a syntax error. Mode (b) means the syntax phase never even sees a large share of real occurrences.
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/syntax/fix_div_rem.ex and test/syntax/fix_div_rem_test.exs — it is the live Credence.Syntax.FixDivRem minus two hunks, and swapping it in trades correct call/dotted right operands for broken ones; then file a SEPARATE P1 bug against the LIVE /home/kamil/projects/credence/lib/syntax/fix_div_rem.ex, whose regex fix silently changes program values (`low + (high - low) div 2` -> `div(low + (high - low), 2)`, mid(10,20)=10 not 15) and mangles tuples/`if`/`fn` lines; the real remedy for both is a token-level rewrite anchored to the parser-reported column that re-parses its own output, plus dropping the line-regex analyze (which cannot see that `n div 2` parses as `n(div(2))`).
reconciliation_note: The live-rule defect this verdict raised is repaired — commit 2964ab4: FixDivRem no longer swallows def/defp heads and no longer rewrites inside string literals.

caught_by: Credence.Syntax.FixDoBlockFusion (detection only — it flags the line but its repair is wrong; see evidence)
failure_mode: Real and correctly phase-filed: a generator writes `do = expr` where keyword-position `do: expr` belongs (`def f(x), do = x + 1`, `for x <- list, do = x + 1 do ... end`), mistaking the keyword for an assignment. Elixir's tokenizer rejects it — `unexpected reserved word: "do"` at the `do` token — so the file does not parse at all and nothing downstream (compiler, dialyzer, credo, pattern/semantic phases) ever sees the module.
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/syntax/fix_do_equals_keyword_syntax.ex and its two tests; then file a separate one-line follow-up against the LIVE /home/kamil/projects/credence/lib/syntax/fix_do_block_fusion.ex to widen @comma_do_midline to `~r/,[ \t]*do[ \t]*=[ \t]*(?=\S)|,[ \t]*do[ \t]+(?!do\b)(?=\S)/`, which turns its current corrupting `, do: = expr` output into correct `, do: expr` for both the plain and the compound form (verified above).

failure_mode: As encoded: "ETS match spec variables written as atoms (`:'$1'`) instead of charlists (`~c\"$1\"`), causing the parse error `unexpected token: \"$\"`." Both halves are backwards. `:'$1'` is a valid single-quoted Elixir atom, identical to `:\"$1\"`, and the atom IS the correct ETS match-spec variable (Erlang `'$1'`); `~c\"$1\"` is the charlist `[36,49]`, which is never a match-spec variable. The construct emits no error at all — only a `severity: :warning` single-quote deprecation. The rule's "repair" is an atom-to-charlist type change that silently turns a working `:ets.select` into one that matches nothing. (The real defect in the field sample its test transcribes is unrelated: an unterminated quoted atom `:'_}` on that line, which swallows the rest of the line and is what actually produces the `unexpected token: \"$\"` at column 42.)
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/semantic/fix_ets_match_spec_atom_variables.ex and both its test files, and catalogue nothing from it — the construct it targets is correct Elixir and its fix replaces the right value with a wrong one; separately, if anyone wants the one real signal seen here, the uncaught `severity: :warning` "single quotes around atoms are deprecated" diagnostic is a distinct, trivially-safe `:'X'` -> `:"X"` rewrite that no live rule handles, but it must be filed as a new rule, not as a salvage of this one.

caught_by: elixir-compiler (hard :error diagnostic, build fails); at dispatch level the live rule Credence.Semantic.FixCaseBranchAssignmentScope claims the diagnostic first and no-ops
failure_mode: Unbound Elixir variable written in ETS match-spec position. The model writes `:ets.match(table, {name, :_, :"$1"})` (or `[{evicted_key, _}] = :ets.match(t, {evicted_key, :"$1"})`) intending the bare lowercase word to act as a capture slot the way `:"$1"` does — an Erlang-match-spec/pattern-position confusion. Mechanism: in Elixir a bare identifier in an *expression* (the 2nd arg to :ets.match is an ordinary data term, not a pattern) must already be bound. Observable consequence: hard compile error `undefined variable "name"`, module does not compile, build fails. Verified real by execution. Secondary, related failure the rule half-understands: even when the variable *is* bound, `:ets.match/2` returns lists-of-bindings (`[[:k, 1]]`), not tuples, so a tuple LHS raises MatchError at runtime.
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/semantic/fix_ets_match_spec_variable_in_comprehension.ex and its two test files; no live-set change is needed since the compiler already fails the build loudly on this error, but record in the catalogue that (a) the for-comprehension repair `:ets.match(t, {:"$1", :_, :"$2"}) |> Enum.map(fn [a,b] -> ... end)` is verified-correct and worth reusing if semantic dispatch ever gains fall-through, and (b) the broad `undefined variable` matcher on FixCaseBranchAssignmentScope is a live dispatch monopoly that silently swallows this and every other undefined-variable diagnostic.

failure_mode: `:ets.new/2` is called with a binary (usually a string interpolation) as the table-name argument — `:ets.new("#{name}_data", [:set, :named_table])`. ETS requires an atom name. The construct parses, compiles with zero diagnostics, and raises `ArgumentError "1st argument: not an atom"` on every single call. Because table creation is normally done in `init/1`, the observable consequence is a supervisor restart loop / `:max_restarts` shutdown at boot, with no ETS-specific message in the crash reason — the module never runs at all, so the failure has whole-subsystem blast radius. The mechanism is a cross-language habit: names as strings, plus Elixir's `"#{}"` being the reflex interpolation form when `:"#{}"` is required.
action: Delete lib/semantic/fix_ets_new_string_name.ex and its two tests (unreachable — fabricated diagnostic), and file the failure mode for a NEW pattern-phase rule: the target compiles cleanly with zero diagnostics, so pattern is the only phase that can see it; check/2 should match the AST call `{{:., _, [:ets, :new]}, _, [arg, _opts]}` where arg is a binary literal or interpolation (`{:<<>>, _, _}` / bare binary), which is unconditionally an ArgumentError — no false positives, since ETS always requires an atom there. Ship it report-only first (per finding 1, do not port this fix); if a fix is later added it must be the AST-scoped rewrite of that one argument node to atom interpolation (`:"#{...}"`), verified above to produce the intended atom, never the whole-line regex.

failure_mode: The `{:keypos, N}` tuple in an `:ets.new/2` options list gets flattened into two bare list elements — `:ets.new(:t, [:named_table, :set, :public, :keypos, 1])`. The list is a syntactically valid list of atoms plus an integer, so it parses and compiles with zero diagnostics; ETS validates options at runtime and every call raises `ArgumentError: errors were found at the given arguments: * 2nd argument: invalid options`. In a GenServer/Supervisor `init/1` (the usual site for table creation) this surfaces as a start-up/restart loop, not as an ETS error, so the observable consequence is misattributed. Same construct family as the live `no_hallucinated_ets_keytype_option` (bogus option) but a different defect (well-formed option, wrong shape).
action: Delete lib/syntax/fix_ets_options_bare_keypos.ex and its two tests, and file the failure mode as a NEW pattern-phase (AST) rule: prewalk for `{{:., _, [:ets, :new]}, _, [_name, opts_list]}` and flag when the literal options list contains a bare `:keypos` atom element (optionally with an integer element following); fix by folding the pair into `{:keypos, N}`, or report-only if the following element is not a literal integer. Do NOT re-file it in semantic — the compile-time diagnostic slot is already taken by Credence.Semantic.NoHallucinatedEtsKeytypeOption (priority 500, first-match-only dispatch) whose fix no-ops on this input, and the common runtime-call case emits no diagnostic at all.

failure_mode: Python/JS-transplanted block scoping in `if`: the model assigns the same variable in both branches of a standalone `if` and then reads it after `end`. Elixir branch bindings do not leak, so the read is unbound. Observable consequence, verified: `error: undefined variable "new_service"` at the use site and the module fails to compile (CompileError, "cannot compile module M"). The sibling variant — the variable IS bound before the `if` — is worse: it compiles, the conditional becomes a silent no-op (the post-`if` read sees the pre-`if` value), and the only signal is a `variable "x" is unused (there is a variable with the same name in the context...)` warning.
action: Delete lib/semantic/fix_if_branch_assignment_scope.ex and its two tests, then file a catalogue item to extend the already-live Credence.Semantic.FixCaseBranchAssignmentScope (it already owns the `undefined variable "x"` dispatch slot, so a separate module can never fire) with an `if`/`unless`/`cond` clause: reuse its existing stmt_spans_line? line anchor and should_report?/2 gate, add branch extraction for `{{:__block__,_,[:do]}, body}` + `{{:__block__,_,[:else]}, body}`, and require the assignment to be the branch's LAST expression before hoisting; separately catalogue a warning-severity rule for the compiling shadowing variant keyed on "there is a variable with the same name in the context", which must be prioritized ahead of Credence.Semantic.UnusedVariable (proved above to underscore it and cement the no-op).

disposition: delete-implementation-dead — the module is dead in its filed phase (target parses; syntax phase never runs it) and actively corrupts `@doc`/`@moduledoc` heredocs on the only files it ever does run on (reproduced). The failure mode IS real and IS uncaught (reproduced: 0/90 semantic rules match, `Credence.analyze` returns `valid: true` on non-compiling source) — but it does not warrant a standalone new rule. Record it instead as a one-line amendment to the EXISTING catalogue entry for the shared `misplaced operator ->` diagnostic (cluster 13, line 226), naming all four shapes that emit the byte-identical message (if-inline-`else:` + multi-line `case`; if-inline-`else:` + multi-line `cond`; `try ... after <pattern> -> ...`; `def f(x) -> expr`), plus the note that the `def f(x), do:` + block variant lands on a different diagnostic entirely. The architectural constraint to record with it: `match?/1` is source-blind and dispatch is first-match, so whoever eventually claims that slot must build ONE owner rule that dispatches internally on AST shape — never four competing rules, and never a broad-match/no-op fix.
failure_mode: Inline keyword `if cond, do: v, else:` whose `else:` value is written as a multi-line `case ... do ... end` on the following lines. Elixir's parser binds `else: case x` (a `case` node with NO body) as the keyword value and then attaches the trailing `do ... end` as a THIRD argument to `if`, producing `if/3` with the `->` clauses orphaned in arg 3. The file parses cleanly, then fails to compile with `misplaced operator ->`. Observable consequence: a hard compile error, positioned on the first `->` line rather than on the `if`, with no rule anywhere in credence able to repair it — the LLM retry budget is spent instead.
action: Delete /home/kamil/projects/credence_evolution/lib/syntax/fix_if_inline_else_case_block.ex and its two tests (dead in its filed phase, and actively corrupts @doc/@moduledoc text on the only files it ever runs on), but file the failure mode for a NEW SEMANTIC rule: match?/1 on `String.contains?(msg, "misplaced operator ->")` with severity :error, then in fix/2 parse the source with Sourceror (it parses) and repair ONLY when the node enclosing the diagnostic line is `{:if, _, [cond, [do: v, else: {:case, _, [subj]}], [do: [{:->, _, _} | _] = clauses]]}` — i.e. if/3 with a body-less `case` in `else:` — rewriting it to `if cond do v else case subj do clauses end end` via Sourceror and re-parsing the output; no-op on every other `misplaced operator ->` shape (notably `try ... after {a,b} -> ...`, which emits the identical message) and add a should_report?/2 hook so analyze only reports when the fix would change the source. Warn whoever builds it that this diagnostic string is a shared, currently-unclaimed dispatch slot: the first rule to claim it with a broad match?/1 and a no-op fix/2 will kill every sibling (semantic.ex:191 is Enum.find, first match only).

caught_by: elixir-compiler (hard :error diagnostic, verified verbatim below) — but NO live credence rule repairs or even reports it: Credence.Semantic.FixInvalidCaptureWithArguments claims the diagnostic first-match and no-ops, and its should_report?/2 then returns false, so analyze/1 emits [].
failure_mode: LLM writes `&<literal>` — `&true`, `&false`, `&nil`, `&:atom`, `&"str"` — as a constant-function callback (Ruby's `&:sym` block-pass generalised to Elixir's capture operator). Elixir's `&` accepts only `&Mod.fun/arity`, `&fun/arity`, or `&expr(&1,…)`, so the compiler hard-errors with `invalid args for &, expected one of: … Got: true` and the module never loads. The same rule's tests also carry a sibling shape from the field — `&System.monotonic_time(:millisecond)` / `&System.os_time(:second/0)` — a 0-arity thunk written with literal call args, same diagnostic. Real-world consequence: file does not compile; the developer gets no automated repair and, today, not even a reported issue.
action: Delete lib/semantic/fix_invalid_capture_with_literal.ex and its two tests from credence_evolution, and file a NEW semantic rule (do not port this fix). Spec: priority 490 (ties with FixNegatedCaptureWithArity, sorts first by module name, disjoint matchers) so it beats FixInvalidCaptureWithArguments; match?/1 = severity :error AND contains "invalid args for &" AND the `Got:` tail is a bare literal (~r/\nGot: (true|false|nil|:[a-z_]\w*[?!]?|"|\d)/); fix/2 keeps ONLY the first prewalk clause of the old module ({:&,meta,[{:__block__,_,[lit]}]} -> fn _ -> lit end) and DELETES the `&fn` and `&Mod.fun(args)` clauses, which are the corrupting ones; add should_report?/2 = `fix(source,diag) != source`. Before shipping the rewrite arm, resolve the arity guess (PROBE 5): either restrict the rewrite to arity-1 callback positions inferable from the enclosing call, or ship the rule report-only — a reported issue is already strictly better than today's silent [].

caught_by: Credence.Syntax.NoMapArrowSyntaxInTupleBrace — but only the `[{k => v}]` sub-case. The bare `[k => v]` / `[atom() => any()]` case is caught by nothing (live rule returns analyze=[] and a byte-identical fix on it, verified).

failure_mode: Map-arrow container generalisation: an LLM writes `=>` inside bare list brackets — `@spec new() :: [atom() => any()]`, `[k => v]` — because `=>` is a map/Erlang-map operator that only exists inside `%{...}`. Elixir's parser stops at the arrow with `syntax error before: '=>'` (verified: `Code.string_to_quoted("[atom() => any()]") == {:error, {[line: 1, column: 9], "syntax error before: ", "'=>'"}}`). Observable consequence: the whole file fails to compile at parse time, so nothing downstream runs. This is a genuine, correctly-phased syntax failure — unlike most of its rejected siblings, the target really does fail to parse.
action: Delete lib/syntax/fix_map_arrow_in_list_bracket.ex and both its tests from credence_evolution; do NOT accept. Record the failure mode in the catalogue as real-and-partially-uncaught: `=>` in bare list brackets (`[atom() => any()]`, no inner `{`) is a genuine parse error that no live rule repairs. If it is ever rebuilt it must be a fresh syntax rule written to the NoMapArrowSyntaxInTupleBrace template (anchor on the parser-blamed line/column, confirm an `=>` really sits there, locate the enclosing `[`, apply a single container edit, re-parse and confirm the intended node at the edited position) — note for the maintainer that the repair target is genuinely ambiguous (`[k => v]` could mean `%{k => v}` or `[{k, v}]`, which are different types and both parse), which is why I am not filing this as rebuild-later.

failure_mode: Generated Elixir puts a keyword-shorthand entry before an arrow entry inside a map — `%{state: atom(), optional(atom()) => any()}` in a `@type`, or `%{state: :init, optional(k) => v}` in a literal. Elixir requires keyword entries to come last in lists and maps, so this is a hard parse error: `unexpected expression after keyword list. Keyword lists must always come last in lists and maps. ... Syntax error after: ` near `"','"`. Observable consequence: the file never reaches the compiler at all, so nothing downstream (dialyzer, credo, the semantic/pattern phases) ever sees it; the whole module is dark. An information-preserving repair exists and was verified to compile — either arrow-ify the keyword entry (`%{:state => atom(), optional(atom()) => any()}`) or move it last (`%{optional(atom()) => any(), state: atom()}`).
action: Delete lib/syntax/fix_mixed_required_optional_map_keys.ex and both its tests — fix/1 is unsalvageable (unanchored whole-file regex that deletes arbitrary spans, plus a premise that discards the required key rather than reordering it), and analyze/1's message would have to change too, so this is a re-author not a narrow. Then file a NEW syntax-phase rule against the catalogued failure mode, built as a sibling of the live Credence.Syntax.FixKeywordBeforePositionalArgument and reusing its exact discipline: gate on the parse error carrying "unexpected expression after keyword list"; use the parser-reported {line, column} to locate the single offending `%{...}`/`[...]`/`{...}` container; decline outright when the container text contains any of `"` `'` `#` `~` `?` `\` `->`; REORDER the keyword entries (arrow-ify or move last) instead of deleting them; and require that the rewritten container reparses before returning it.

failure_mode: Definition-order alias invisibility for nested modules. A `defmodule Child` nested inside `defmodule Parent` installs its alias LEXICALLY at the point of the nested `defmodule`; any code above it that writes `Child.fun(...)` expands to top-level `Elixir.Child`, which does not exist. Mechanism: Elixir expands aliases at compile time even inside `def` bodies, so "append helpers at the bottom" (fine for plain functions) silently breaks for nested modules. Observable consequence: the file COMPILES — warning only, build stays green under normal settings — and the process dies in production with `UndefinedFunctionError: function Coordinator.start_link/0 is undefined (module Coordinator is not available)`. Executed and confirmed. The compiler already names the exact repair in a "Did you mean" block.
action: Delete lib/semantic/fix_nested_module_short_reference.ex and both its tests (wrong diagnostic, and string-corrupting on the only message it can reach), and file the failure mode as a NEW semantic rule: match? requires severity :warning AND "is undefined (module " AND " is not available or is yet to be defined)" AND a "Did you mean:" block whose sole suggestion ends in "." <> flagged_call (i.e. the suggested MFA is the flagged one with a module prefix); fix/2 then replaces only the alias at the diagnostic's reported {line, col} with the suggested fully-qualified path, AST-scoped and re-parsed — never a whole-source regex. failure_mode: `when` written as a comma-separated *filter* in a `for` comprehension — `for {name, price, _qty} <- items, when price > 100 do ... end`. Observable consequence: hard parse failure `{[line: 1, column: 35], "syntax error before: ", "'when'"}` — the file never reaches the compiler. (The moduledoc's "Python-ism" attribution is FALSE: Python has no `when`; its comprehension filter is `if`.)

failure_mode: Stated: a `case`/`do…end` block used bare as a map-literal value (`%{k: case x do … end, k2: v}`) is claimed to be "non-idiomatic" and to make parsers/tooling "choke". Executed check: it is ordinary, correct Elixir — it parses, produces an AST byte-identical to the parenthesized form, evaluates identically, and `mix format` (Code.format_string!) emits exactly the BARE form, stripping the parens the rule inserts. There is no error, no warning, no wrong value, no tooling failure. The rule's premise is false. The genuinely-real neighbour in this family is the KEYWORD form of a block expression inside a container (`%{a: case x, do: (…), b: 2}`, `%{a: if x, do: 1, else: 2}`, `%{a: for x <- xs, into: %{}, do: {x,x}}`), which is a true parse error ("unexpected comma. Parentheses are required to solve ambiguity inside containers"). That is a different construct and the rule does not target it.

failure_mode: A function definition emitted without the `def`/`defp` keyword — `init(opts) do … end` written directly in a module body (Python/Ruby-style). Elixir parses it as a compile-time local *call* of arity N+1 (the do-block is an extra argument), so the module fails to compile with `undefined function init/2 (there is no such import)`. The arity being one higher than intended is the tell. Observable consequence: the module never compiles, and no live rule repairs it. A darker variant exists: inside a DSL module where a `use`d macro of the same name/arity IS imported, the missing-`def` form compiles silently and defines something else entirely.
action: Delete `lib/semantic/no_bare_function_def_syntax.ex` and its two tests from credence_evolution, and file the failure mode as a NEW semantic rule to build: match `~r/^undefined function (\w+)\/([1-9]\d*) \(there is no such import\)$/` at default priority 500 (do NOT lower it — MissingUseExunitCase must keep test/2 and the arity≥1 guard leaves init/0 to NoModuleLevelInit; only plug/1 is taken from UndefinedFunction, where its fix is already a no-op), then in `fix/2` parse the source with Sourceror (it parses — this is a compile error, not a parse error), locate the call node at the diagnostic's {line, col}, and prepend `def ` ONLY when every positional argument is a bare variable (`init(opts)`, `handle_call(msg, from, state)`), refusing when any argument is a literal (`get("/ping")`, `plug(:match)`, `test("works")`, `pipeline(:browser)`, `field(:name, :string)`) — that literal-vs-variable split is what separates a missing `def` from a missing `use`; re-parse the output before returning.

failure_mode: A GenServer `init/1` returns a bare value (map, struct, list) instead of an OTP-tagged `{:ok, state}`. `use GenServer` + `def init(_opts), do: %{count: 0}` compiles with zero diagnostics; at runtime `GenServer.start_link/3` exits with `bad return value: %{count: 0}`, so a supervised child aborts the supervisor's whole start sequence at boot. The construct is `def init/1` in a module with `use GenServer`/`@behaviour GenServer` whose body's last expression is a literal that is not `{:ok, _}`, `{:ok, _, _}`, `{:stop, _}` or `:ignore`. failure_mode: LLMs trained on Python emit a bare, argument-less `return` on its own line as an early exit inside an Elixir block. Elixir has no early-exit construct; the parser reads `return` as a variable reference, so the file compiles to `undefined variable "return"` (error, position on the `return` token) and the module never loads. Distinct from the sibling form `return value`, which produces `undefined function return/1`. Observable consequence: the generated module is uncompilable, and — because there is no early exit in the language at all — no line-level edit can restore the intended control flow; only restructuring the body into `if/else` (condition inverted for `unless`) or `with` preserves intent.

failure_mode: Bare `&identifier` written as a callback — `&` capture applied to a name with no `/arity` and no `&1` body (e.g. `Map.update!(m, :key, &new_value)`, `Enum.map(list, &transform)`). failure_mode: LLM-generated code puts a `catch` clause inside a `receive` block (try/catch confusion): `receive do {:ok, r} -> ... catch :exit, _ -> {:error, :timeout} after 5_000 -> ... end`. failure_mode: Generated Elixir calls a module that does not exist (hallucinated namespace, e.g. `MyApp.Repo.insert!/1` in a self-contained snippet). The compiler emits a *warning* only, so the file compiles; under `--warnings-as-errors` the build fails, and without it the program compiles cleanly and dies at call time with `UndefinedFunctionError: function MyApp.Repo.insert!/1 is undefined (module MyApp.Repo is not available)`. Real and common (it is the 23-member hallucinated-API cluster in the catalogue). What is NOT real is this rule's premise about the remedy: it treats the warning as noise to be silenced with `@compile {:no_warn_undefined, Mod}`, which is only correct for genuinely-optional runtime deps. For hallucinated modules — the corpus this tool serves — suppression deletes the single compile-time signal and converts a caught defect into an uncaught runtime crash. There is no safe automated repair for the real failure mode: you cannot synthesise the missing module.

failure_mode: Python/JS scoping intuition applied to Elixir `if`/`else`: the LLM assigns the same variable in both branches (`if x > t do count = 1 else count = 0 end`) and then reads it after the block. Elixir scopes branch bindings to the branch, so the trailing read is unbound. Observable consequence: hard compile failure — `error: undefined variable "count"` at the read site, preceded by two `variable "count" is unused` warnings at the two assignment sites. The correct repair is to hoist: `count = if x > t do 1 else 0 end`. This is the `if` sibling of the `case` variant that live FixCaseBranchAssignmentScope already repairs; the `if` (and `cond`) form is repaired by nothing.

failure_mode: Two distinct things are conflated, and the one the rule names does not exist. (a) The claimed mode — "Date.utc_today/1 is hallucinated by LLMs" — is FALSE: `Date.utc_today(calendar)` is a real, exported, documented arity (Date.__info__(:functions) => [utc_today: 0, utc_today: 1]). No arity/undefined-function error ever occurs. (b) The genuine defect visible in the rule's own field sample is different and real: generated code destructures the %Date{} struct returned by Date.utc_today into a tuple pattern (`case Date.utc_today(ts) do {y,m,d} -> ...`), i.e. tuple-destructuring a struct-returning stdlib call. failure_mode: An LLM defines a local `defp/def to_string/1` (a stock key/value normaliser) inside a module that also calls `to_string(x)` unqualified. failure_mode: Python-style `for ... do ... else ... end` transplanted into Elixir. Elixir's `for` accepts `:into`, `:uniq`, `:reduce` but never `:else`; the construct is syntactically valid (it parses as a keyword option to the `for` macro) and dies only at expansion with the error-severity diagnostic `unsupported option :else given to for`, followed by `cannot compile module X (errors have been logged)`. The `else` body is dead code by construction — Python's for/else fires when the loop finishes without `break`, and Elixir comprehensions have no `break` — so the correct repair is to drop the `:else` option entirely. Observable consequence: hard compile failure of the whole module, with a diagnostic that points at the `for` header (line 3, col 5) rather than at the `else` keyword, so the user is told an option is unsupported without being shown which line to delete.

failure_mode: Ruby/Python control-flow transfer: an LLM writes `if <cond> do ... elsif <cond> do ... else ... end`. `elsif` is not an Elixir keyword, so the parser reads it as a call and the enclosing `do` never closes — the file fails to parse with a misleading "missing terminator: end / hint: it looks like the \"do\" on line 1 does not have a matching \"end\"" pointing at the `if`, not at the `elsif`. Observable consequence: the whole file is uncompilable and the reported line is wrong. The behaviour-preserving repair is a `cond do` chain with `true ->` for `else` (and an explicit `true -> nil` when there is no `else`, since `if` without `else` yields nil while `cond` raises CondClauseError).

failure_mode: Validation-by-`raise` inside a `GenServer.handle_cast/2` callback. `GenServer.cast/2` is fire-and-forget: it returns `:ok` to the caller *before* the handler runs, so when the handler raises on bad input the caller is told the operation succeeded while the server process dies with all of its state and the write is silently lost. Observable consequence: `LWW.add(pid, :x, -5)` returns `:ok`; 200ms later the server is dead (`Process.alive?/1 == false`) with `{%ArgumentError{}, ...}`; every subsequent call to that pid exits `:noproc`. Zero compiler diagnostics. Independent of this implementation.

failure_mode: Deferred-reply protocol violation in a GenServer `handle_call/3`: the callback destructures the caller's pid out of `from` (`{caller_pid, _ref} = _from`), returns `{:noreply, state}`, and delivers the result with `send(caller_pid, result)` — often from a spawned Task. `GenServer.call/3` waits in a selective receive keyed on the alias/monitor reference it created, so only `GenServer.reply(from, r)` completes it. Observable consequence: the caller blocks for the full timeout and then exits `{:timeout, {GenServer, :call, ...}}`, and the stray raw message is left in the caller's mailbox where its next unrelated `receive` consumes it as its own. Nothing is logged at the point of the bug and the compiler emits zero diagnostics — it is a hang plus cross-talk, not a crash.

failure_mode: Generated GenServer code passes the caller's bare PID through a `cast` message (`GenServer.cast(server, {:execute, self(), ...})`) and then calls `GenServer.reply(caller, msg)` inside `handle_cast/2`. `GenServer.reply/2` requires the `{pid, [:alias | ref]}` from-tuple that only `handle_call/3` receives; a bare PID hits no clause in `:gen.reply/2`. Observable consequence: the server process dies with `FunctionClauseError` on the first cast (logged), the caller — sitting in a bare `receive` with no `after` — blocks forever, and any other client of that GenServer loses the process. Zero compile-time diagnostics; the code compiles cleanly.

failure_mode: A GenServer callback builds its reply tuple and then pipes it into a state helper — `{:noreply, %{state | count: state.count + 1}} |> maybe_process()` — so `maybe_process/1` receives `{:noreply, state}`, not the bare state map. Mechanism: `|>` inserts the *whole* left expression as arg 1; the tuple constructor binds looser than the pipe reads. Observable consequence: `BadMapError` (or `FunctionClauseError`) on the first call to that callback, killing the GenServer process; under a supervisor it presents as a restart loop, not as a pipe bug. Corollary confirmed by probe: if the helper is a pure pass-through (`defp maybe_process(s), do: s`) the shape is harmless — the tuple flows straight through as the callback return — so the defect is helper-dependent, not shape-dependent.

Unlike Python/Ruby/JS, Elixir refuses the ambiguity: the module fails to compile with `imported M.f/N conflicts with local function` (arity-exact; fires regardless of def/defp or definition order; only fires if there is an unqualified call site). Observable consequence: the whole module fails to compile.

failure_mode: `Map.update(map, key, <constant>, fun)` where the callback's per-call contribution is data-dependent (a `case type do "credit" -> e + amount; "debit" -> e - amount end`, or plainly `&(&1 + amount)`). The construct's real semantics: when the key is ABSENT the default is inserted VERBATIM and the callback is never invoked. So the first transaction for each key is silently discarded and replaced by the constant. Observable consequence: every account/bucket is off by exactly its first contribution, with zero compiler diagnostics, zero exceptions, and a plausible-looking result. Executed: a credit-100 / debit-30 / debit-20 ledger yields -50 where 50 is correct; `Enum.reduce([10,20,30], %{}, &Map.update(&2, :k, 0, fn e -> e + &1 end))` yields 50 where 60 is correct. Note the moduledoc's stated mechanism ("the first debit evaluates 0 - amount") is FALSE — the callback never runs on the default — but the bug it points at is real by a different mechanism. Mechanically checkable invariant: a constant default is only correct when it equals what the callback would produce from the operation's identity element.

failure_mode: Nested capture operators: an inner `&(...)` or `&Mod.fun/arity` appearing inside an outer `&(...)` capture. failure_mode: `|>` assumed to bind tighter than `in`. failure_mode: A `defp` helper called *unqualified* from inside a `quote` block in a `defmacro`. `quote` does not hygienize function calls — the call is emitted into and resolved in the CALLER's context, not the defining module's. Two verified consequences: (1) every `require M; M.macro(...)` call site fails to compile with `undefined function check_order/2 (expected C1 to define such a function or for it to be imported, but none are available)`; (2) if the caller happens to define a same-named function, the macro SILENTLY calls the caller's implementation (verified: `:CALLERS_OWN_IMPL` returned, zero errors, zero warnings at the caller). In both cases the defining module's only signal is `function check_order/2 is unused` — a warning that actively misdescribes a used-but-unreachable function as dead code. Correct remediation is to qualify the call inside the quote (`__MODULE__.check_order(...)`) and make the helper public; promoting `defp`→`def` alone is NOT sufficient.

failure_mode: LLM-generated `Plug.Router` modules reference a bare `options` variable inside a route-handler `do` block (`post "/webhook" do store = Keyword.get(options, :store) ... end`). Plug.Router compiles a route body into `fn var!(conn), var!(opts) -> _ = var!(opts); body end` (corpus/plug/lib/plug/router.ex:611) — the ONLY two names it injects are `conn` and `opts`, never `options`. Since Elixir 1.15 an unbound name is a hard error, so the module fails to compile with `undefined variable "options"` at the exact position. Observable consequence: hard compile failure, loudly and precisely located. There is no `conn.private[:plug_router_opts]` key anywhere in Plug (grep over the whole package: 0 hits); the documented escape hatch is `:copy_opts_to_assign`, which writes to `conn.assigns` — the rule's moduledoc premise is false. Worse, the value the author wanted is not mechanically recoverable: with a plain `plug :dispatch` the injected `opts` is `[]` (the dispatch plug's own opts), and only `plug :dispatch, builder_opts()` makes it the router's init opts — verified V1 -> "[]", V2 -> "[store: :s]". So a correct repair requires editing the plug pipeline too, not just binding a name.

failure_mode: A generated module leaves behind a `defp` that nothing calls. Elixir emits `warning: function <name>/<arity> is unused` at the definition line; under `--warnings-as-errors` (or `mix compile --warnings-as-errors` in CI) that warning fails the build. The construct is a dead private helper — usually an abandoned intermediate step of a refactor, or a callback the author meant to schedule by name (`:timer.apply_after(ms, __MODULE__, :do_cleanup, [pid])`, `spawn/3`, an `{M,F,A}` child spec) and left private, in which case the same warning misdescribes the defect: the function is not dead, it is unreachable-by-MFA because `defp` is not exported, and the correct repair is `def`, not deletion (verified: `apply(__MODULE__, :secret, [])` on a `defp` raises "function ApplyDyn2.secret/0 is undefined or private").

failure_mode: LLM writes Elixir's `div`/`rem` as infix operators (Python `//`/`%`, Haskell `div` habit): `expected_sum = n * (n + 1) div 2`. Mechanism: `div`/`rem` are functions, not operators. Two distinct observable consequences, confirmed by execution: (1) when the left operand ends in `)` or is a call/expression, it is a hard PARSE error — `{[line: 1, column: 28], "syntax error before: ", "'div'"}`; (2) when both operands are bare identifiers (`a div b`), it PARSES as the unparenthesized call `a(div(b))` and instead dies at compile time with `undefined function a/1` + `undefined function div/1`. The failure mode is real. Case (1) is fully owned by the live Credence.Syntax.FixDivRem; case (2) is out of scope for any syntax-phase rule and is at least detected today by live Credence.Semantic.UndefinedFunction.

failure_mode: "Cons tail bound in the function head, then immediately re-destructured in the body: `def f([h | t]) do [x | _] = t; ...`". Executed, this construct is CORRECT Elixir — it compiles and returns the right answer for every list of length >= 2 (`Before.d_check([1,2])` -> `{1, 2}`). It is a verbosity/style preference, not an error. The rule's premise is that `[h | t]` + body-destructure and `[h, x | _rest]` are interchangeable; they are not — the head form accepts 1-element and improper lists (raising MatchError inside the body), the folded form rejects them at dispatch. The only adjacent REAL error (a MatchError when the caller passes a 1-element list) is not repaired by the fix; it is merely renamed to FunctionClauseError, so the program still crashes on exactly the same inputs.

failure_mode: `length(list) > 0` used as a non-emptiness test in a clause guard — a Python/Ruby `len(x) > 0` idiom transferred to Elixir. Observable consequence: measured 303715 us vs 57 us for 50 guard evaluations on a 3-million-element list (~5300x); on a very long or lazily-grown list this is a latency cliff, and it is a real Elixir 1.20.2 compiler warning, so it is also permanent build noise. Real, and independent of this implementation.
